mainClaim: Four-day workweeks maintain or increase productivity while dramatically improving employee wellbeing
evidence: The UK four-day week pilot (Autonomy report, February 2023) covered 61 companies and about 2,900 workers from June to December 2022. Of those companies, 56 (92%) were continuing with a four-day week afterward and 18 had made it permanent. Revenue stayed broadly the same, rising 1.4% on average over the trial across the 23 organisations that reported it (weighted by company size); against a comparable earlier six-month period, 24 organisations averaged a 35% increase. The number of staff leaving participating companies fell by 57%. Among employees, 71% reported reduced burnout and 39% reported being less stressed.
supportingPoints: Reduced hours force efficiency gains and elimination of time-wasting meetings
Three-day weekends allow full mental recovery and prevent burnout
Attraction/retention tool in competitive talent markets
Environmental impact: reduced commuting and office energy use

sourceMetadata.title: The results are in: the UK's four-day week pilot
sourceMetadata.institution: Autonomy, with researchers at Boston College and University College Dublin
sourceMetadata.methodology: Pilot of self-selected UK employers with company metrics and employee surveys

limitations: The cited source is a pilot report, not a peer-reviewed paper, and the participating companies chose to take part. The report does not support the Iceland or '45 points' figures this record previously cited. Results vary by industry - difficult for 24/7 operations or customer-facing roles. May not work for hourly workers paid for time. Requires significant organizational restructuring. Long-term effects beyond 12 months less studied.
